title: 3D-Printed Brushless DC Motor
summary: A custom 36N40P fractional-slot motor built to connect electromagnetic theory with physical prototyping.
description: A custom 36N40P fractional-slot motor built to connect electromagnetic theory with physical prototyping.
objectives: Design, fabricate, and characterize a custom 36N40P fractional-slot brushless DC (BLDC) motor from first principles, exploring how winding configurations, magnetic flux, and mechanical design influence motor performance for future robotic actuators.
contributions: Modelled the motor assembly in SolidWorks and fabricated custom components using PLA Pro, designing around a 10010 laminated stator core.
Hand-wound 36 stator coils using six parallel strands of 26 AWG magnet wire per winding, connected in a Wye configuration.
Developed a low-cost back-EMF testing method using a power drill, smartphone RPM measurement, and induced voltage measurements between motor phases.

process.title: Mechanical Design & Fabrication
process.body: Designed the motor housing and rotor assembly in SolidWorks, accounting for bearing placement, stator alignment, and magnet positioning. Iteratively 3D-printed components to verify tolerances and achieve a functional assembly.

process.title: Electromagnetic Design
process.body: Selected a 36-slot, 40-pole configuration and manually wound the stator. Used multiple parallel strands of thinner magnet wire to improve slot packing and reduce winding resistance while maintaining flexibility during winding.

process.title: Back-EMF Testing & Characterization
process.body: Coupled the motor shaft to a power drill and rotated it at a controlled speed, using a smartphone tachometer app to estimate RPM. With the motor acting as a generator, measured the induced AC voltage between stator phases. Compared the voltage against rotational speed to estimate the motor's back-EMF constant and calculate Kv.

results: Successfully fabricated a functional BLDC motor prototype and characterized its electrical performance using an accessible, low-cost testing setup.
Calculated a speed constant of 443.4 RPM/V, significantly higher than the intended design target.
The elevated Kv suggested insufficient magnetic flux linkage, resulting in a lower-than-desired torque constant and highlighting a limitation in the rotor's magnetic return path.
lessons: Back-EMF testing reinforced the relationship between rotational speed, magnetic flux, and torque production. The next iteration will incorporate a steel rotor back iron or flux ring to provide a lower-reluctance magnetic return path, increase flux linkage, and reduce Kv. Further testing will compare the revised motor's electrical and torque characteristics against the original prototype.
